entry.title: Design Innovation Master's at the University of Bristol

media:group.media:title: Design Innovation Master's at the University of Bristol
media:group.media:description:
Postgraduate Design Innovation master's programmes at the University of Bristol. Learn to use design to tackle complex challenges in business, public services and society, and leave things better than you found them.
What is design innovation? Design innovation uses design approaches such as systems thinking, user research and participatory design to tackle complex challenges across business, technology, society and the environment. At Bristol, four specialist programmes are taught together as one interdisciplinary community.
Which Design Innovation programme is right for you? Drive design-led innovation in business ▸ MSc Design Strategy: use design as a strategic capability to guide organisations and drive transformation. https://www.bristol.ac.uk/study/postgraduate/taught/msc-design-strategy/
Make services and experiences work better for people ▸ MA Service Design: create services that are intuitive, inclusive and meaningful, using service research, journey mapping, service blueprinting and co-design. https://www.bristol.ac.uk/study/postgraduate/tught/ma-service-design/
Shape the future we want to live in ▸ MSc Design Futures: explore, imagine and create better futures through strategic foresight, scenario planning and speculative design. https://www.bristol.ac.uk/study/postgraduate/taught/msc-design-futures/
Create solutions that give back more than they take ▸ MA Regenerative Design: combine living systems thinking, ecology and design practice to tackle challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss and food systems. https://www.bristol.ac.uk/study/postgraduate/taught/ma-regenerative-design/
Do I need a design degree to apply? No, the programmes are open to graduates from any discipline, typically with an upper second-class honours degree or international equivalent.
How are Bristol’s Design Innovation master’s programmes structured? ▸ Shared core units in systems thinking and participatory design, alongside a specialist unit in your chosen programme ▸ Advanced study in your specialism through live projects, studio-based activities and industry-informed challenges ▸ An elective from across the Design Innovation portfolio ▸ A final interdisciplinary Design Innovation Project, tackling a real-world challenge in a multidisciplinary team
What jobs can I get with a Design Innovation master's? Graduates of Bristol’s Design Innovation master’s are prepared for roles across the public, private and third sectors, including: ▸ Design leadership, consultancy and innovation management ▸ Service design, digital transformation and customer experience ▸ Futures consultancy, innovation strategy and policy design ▸ Sustainability and regeneration consultancy, environmental strategy and ESG leadership
Why study design innovation at Bristol? ▸ A Russell Group university, ranked fifth for research in the UK, with 94% of research assessed as world-leading or internationally excellent (REF 2021) ▸ Four design specialisms studied together, so you collaborate across disciplines ▸ Taught at our Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus, with some teaching at Clifton ▸ One year full-time, starting September 2027 ▸ Bristol students and graduates may be eligible for a 25% reduction in tuition fees

entry.title: AMR in Fragile and Conflict Settings | Panel 1: Fragility, Conflict and the Foundations of AMR

media:group.media:title: AMR in Fragile and Conflict Settings | Panel 1: Fragility, Conflict and the Foundations of AMR
media:group.media:description: How do conflict, displacement, weak governance and environmental pressures contribute to antimicrobial resistance (AMR)? This panel explores the foundations of AMR in fragile settings, drawing on lessons from history, healthcare disruption, sanitation challenges and environmental contamination. Speakers discuss why AMR should be understood not only as a clinical issue, but as a consequence of wider social, political and environmental fragility.

entry.title: Trust, Governance and Security in the Fight Against AMR | Panel 2

media:group.media:title: Trust, Governance and Security in the Fight Against AMR | Panel 2
media:group.media:description: This panel examines the systems and institutions that shape the global response to antimicrobial resistance. Discussions explore governance, international coordination, public trust, misinformation, security perspectives and the implications of AMR for modern healthcare. Speakers reflect on the challenges and opportunities of building effective and trusted responses across sectors.

entry.title: AMR's Hidden Impacts: Health, Trauma and Humanitarian Challenges | Panel 3

media:group.media:title: AMR's Hidden Impacts: Health, Trauma and Humanitarian Challenges | Panel 3
media:group.media:description: Antimicrobial resistance affects far more than infectious disease alone. This panel explores the intersections between AMR, conflict-related injuries, humanitarian healthcare, disability and eye health. Speakers discuss practical innovations in microbiology and diagnostics, alongside the growing burden of resistant infections in fragile and resource-constrained environments.

entry.title: Patients, Surveillance and Future AMR Risks | Panel 4

media:group.media:title: Patients, Surveillance and Future AMR Risks | Panel 4
media:group.media:description: What can patient experiences tell us about the future of antimicrobial resistance? This discussion considers AMR from patient, health system and security perspectives, exploring access to care, surveillance, preparedness and the challenges faced in conflict-affected settings. The panel reflects on how local AMR threats may foreshadow wider global risks.

entry.title: Beyond One Health: Data, Technology and AMR Surveillance | Panel 5

media:group.media:title: Beyond One Health: Data, Technology and AMR Surveillance | Panel 5
media:group.media:description: This panel explores how surveillance systems for antimicrobial resistance must evolve to meet the challenges of fragile and conflict-affected environments. Discussions focus on data, technology, diagnostics and systems thinking, while considering how surveillance can be designed to support action, protection and better decision-making in resource-constrained settings.

entry.title: From Discussion to Action: Policy, Accountability and the Future of AMR | Panel 6

media:group.media:title: From Discussion to Action: Policy, Accountability and the Future of AMR | Panel 6
media:group.media:description: The final panel focuses on the policies, partnerships and investments needed to address antimicrobial resistance effectively. Speakers discuss governance, accountability, financing and implementation, while exploring how AMR can serve as a catalyst for stronger systems, international collaboration and long-term resilience in fragile settings.

entry.title: MSc Urban Science at the University of Bristol | Data Science for Cities

media:group.media:title: MSc Urban Science at the University of Bristol | Data Science for Cities
media:group.media:description:
MSc Urban Science at the University of Bristol: learn to see cities differently, using urban theory, data science and GeoAI to solve real-world challenges. https://www.bristol.ac.uk/study/postgraduate/taught/msc-urban-science
Cities are at the centre of today's most pressing global challenges. Our MSc Urban Science helps you understand the relationships between people, infrastructure, data and the environment, so you can see not just what's happening in a city, but why, and how to change it.
What will I study? ▸ Core units in urban theory and urban analytics ▸ Applied work on sustainability, risk and consultancy-based projects tackling real urban challenges ▸ Optional units in data science, GIS, remote sensing, machine learning and climate risks ▸ An independent research project combining theory, data analysis and applied problem-solving
Who is it for? Graduates in any social science, science, mathematics or professional degree, such as medicine, architecture, planning or engineering. Applicants from other subjects with experience in data science, GIS, coding, modelling or statistics are considered case by case.
Where can it take me? Careers in urban and transport planning, infrastructure and sustainability consultancy, government, technology companies, NGOs and data analytics, or doctoral research in urban, environmental or geospatial science.
Why study Urban Science at Bristol? ▸ Taught in the School of Geographical Sciences, top 15 in the world for Geography (QS World University Rankings by Subject 2026) ▸ Bridges the gap between technical, data science programmes and urban studies degrees ▸ Close links to Bristol’s Planetary Urban Sciences Lab (+Lab) ▸ One year full-time or two years part-time, on our Clifton campus ▸ Bursaries available for outstanding overseas applicants (see the course page for details)
Find out more and apply: https://www.bristol.ac.uk/study/postgraduate/taught/msc-urban-science/

entry.title: From moth wings to sound absorbers | The Story Behind

media:group.media:title: From moth wings to sound absorbers | The Story Behind
media:group.media:description:
How did a moth in Costa Rica lead to a new generation of sound-absorbing materials?
In the first episode of The Story Behind, we follow Professor Marc Holderied from the biology that started it all to ultra-thin acoustic materials, working prototypes and a University of Bristol spin-out. Inspired by the microscopic structures found on moth wings, the technology is being developed through Attacus Acoustics, with potential applications across buildings, transport, aerospace and manufacturing. The film explores how moths avoid detection by bats, the experiments used to understand how their wings absorb sound, and how this research could help reduce noise in everyday spaces.

entry.title: Training health workers to have more effective vaccine conversations

media:group.media:title: Training health workers to have more effective vaccine conversations
media:group.media:description:
The best vaccine conversations aren't just about sharing information. People with vaccine concerns are shaped by underlying psychological drivers, or "attitude roots", that influence how they interpret information and misinformation. Effective conversations start with understanding these drivers, building trust, and providing the right information in the right way to support informed decision-making.
🩺💬
Dr Emma Anderson, Professor Stephan Lewandowsky, and Dr Ginny Gould share how JITSUVAX Training, a University of Bristol social venture, brings specialist psychological expertise to enhance health workers’ skills and confidence to address vaccine misinformation effectively.
Developed from international research led by the University of Bristol, JITSUVAX Training trains health workers with practical tools to identify and address the psychological drivers underpinning vaccine concerns using empathetic communication approaches and insights from cognitive psychology. Participants learn how to correct misinformation, avoid arguments and protect positive patient relationships, with a memorable conversation framework (the ‘Empathetic Refutational Interview’) shown to build trust and increase vaccine acceptance.
Since launching, the programme has trained hundreds of people across the healthcare sector, and the expert team is expanding training delivery across the UK and building links internationally with the World Health Organisation.
Find out more and get in touch through the venture's website: https://jitsuvaxtraining.com/
